Arose
a-rōz'
v. (preterite of arise: rose up, stood up, set out; rendering Hebrew qum, Greek anistemi)
Preterite of arise, from the Saxon arisan. Hebrew qum means to stand up and very often to begin acting — the Hebrew narrative idiom he arose and went marks decision, not merely posture — and Greek anistemi is the standard verb both for getting up and for resurrection.

Biblical Definition

Arose is one of the great hinge words of biblical narrative. In Hebrew idiom a man arises before he acts, so the word marks the moment resolve becomes motion. The prodigal's repentance turns on it: having said I will arise and go to my father, the text records that “he arose, and came to his father” (Luke 15:20), and the distance between resolution and arising is where most repentance dies. Deborah's song uses it of God raising up a deliverer in a collapsing nation: the villages ceased “until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel” (Judges 5:7). Mark uses it for the immediate evidence of Christ's authority: at his word the palsied man “immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went forth before them all” (Mark 2:12), the healing proving the forgiveness that had just been pronounced. And the word can mark flight as easily as obedience, for Jonah too “rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” (Jonah 1:3) — the same decisive verb, aimed the wrong way. Its greatest weight is that the Greek behind it, anistemi, is the resurrection verb; the ordinary rising of a man from his bed and the rising of the dead are named alike.

Webster 1828 Definition

Preterite of arise — rose up, and in Hebrew idiom, set about acting. The prodigal arose and came to his father; and the Greek behind it is the New Testament's resurrection verb.

expand to see more

AROSE, pret. of arise. [Sax. arisan.] Rose up; got up from a sitting, lying or kneeling posture.

2. Proceeded; issued; sprang; as, a dispute arose among them.

3. Began to act; set out; as, he arose and went on his journey.

4. Was raised up by God for a purpose; as, until that I Deborah arose, Judges 5.

5. In Scripture, of the prodigal; as, he arose, and came to his father, Luke 15.

Key Scripture

Luke 15:20 — "And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him."

Judges 5:7 — "The inhabitants of the villages ceased, they ceased in Israel, until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel."

Mark 2:12 — "And immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went forth before them all; insomuch that they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, We never saw it on this fashion."

Jonah 1:3 — "But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word's force is lost by familiarity rather than by attack: a narrative hinge is read as scene-setting, and the decisive step it marks goes unnoticed.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What has weakened is attention. Readers pass over and he arose as stage direction, when in Hebrew narrative it is the point at which intention becomes action. Luke 15 makes the structure visible by giving the sentence twice: first the prodigal says in the far country, I will arise and go to my father, and then the narrative says he arose and came. The whole parable turns in that gap, and the gap is where a great many men live — convinced, resolved, and still in the far country.

The principle to recover is that Scripture regularly makes repentance a matter of rising and moving rather than of feeling. Mark 2:12 shows the same logic in the physical order: Christ pronounces forgiveness, which cannot be seen, and then commands a rising that can, so that the visible arising authenticates the invisible pardon. And because anistemi is also the resurrection verb, every such rising in the Gospels is a small rehearsal of the last one, when all that are in the graves shall hear his voice and shall come forth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qum is to stand up, to arise, and so to set about a thing; it is also the verb of covenant establishment. Greek anistemi is to stand up or raise up, the ordinary resurrection verb, and egeiro is to awaken or raise.

expand to see more

Hebrew qum (H6965) — to arise, to stand, to be established; the narrative hinge verb.

Hebrew talitha cumi — damsel, arise; the Aramaic imperative our Lord spoke over Jairus' daughter.

Greek anistemi (G450) — to stand up, to rise; used of rising from sleep and of resurrection alike.

Greek egeiro (G1453) — to awaken, to raise up; he is not here: for he is risen.

Greek anastasis (G386) — a standing up again, resurrection; the noun formed from anistemi.

Usage

"Of repentance becoming motion: he arose, and came to his father (Luke 15:20)."

"Of a deliverer raised up in a failing nation: until that I Deborah arose (Judges 5:7)."

"Of healing that authenticates pardon: immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went forth (Mark 2:12)."
